ratings.reason: The quoted code shows a real, well-evidenced logic gap — finding_files returning [] for any location that isn't a resolvable path:line means any(x -> x in touched, []) is always false, so a closed finding with policy/architecture-style locations (routine in this domain) can never become a suspect again and is also skipped by unswept's new refusal gate — silently contradicting the stated design guarantee in ARCHITECTURE §6.2/PROTOCOL.md that closed findings regress-check via their own evidence; this is a real, plausibly-hit contradiction between documented intent and implementation rather than an immediate wrong-math/API read, so major rather than blocker.

The regex gap is real and verified (confirmed by reading src/CLI/Config.jl:210 and reproducing the match), and it does fall short of ARCHITECTURE §7.3's own spec ("every .jl script the docs_build command names exists"), but the triggering shape — a docs_build value with a quoted, space-containing .jl filename — appears nowhere in this repo: the fixture, the tool's own config, and the test suite (test/config.jl) all use plain unquoted paths, and every space in the whole fleet lives in root/Dropbox directory names (already handled separately via run_under_round's `dir=root`, not the cmdline string), never in an individual script filename. So the CLAUDE.md space-quoting invariant the finding invokes is about a different class of path than the one this check parses, making the practical trigger narrow and currently hypothetical; and when it did fire, the failure is a loud, immediately diagnosable "file does not exist" error rather than a silent wrong belief.

The diff is real (additionalProperties: true -> {$ref: entry} on both maps), but the practical "hard-fail on an older-tool sidecar/tally" risk is speculative rather than demonstrated: the entry-writing code (Sync.jl's files map, Passes.jl's per_id construction) has always produced exactly the {template,version,sha256} / {act,act_demoted,state,closed_by[,adjudicated_entry]} shape the now-referenced `entry` $def already required (it was just unenforced by the wrapper before), and checking every real historical tally.json in this repo's own `.gbg/rounds/` confirms every entry already conforms to the tightened schema. The one concrete failure path (read_sidecar) is explicitly disclosed with an actionable recovery message ("a sidecar written before its schema was closed; delete it and re-run gbg sync") that the finding itself quotes, undercutting its own "disclosed only in prose, not a compatibility note" framing as the load-bearing complaint. Real and worth a CHANGELOG mention, but not a defect a reader is shown to plausibly hit.

The finding's entire payload is the claim that reversing resolve_function's search order changes which method count a Base-shadowed name resolves to (and can flip a consumer's frozen baseline), but this is structurally false — `pkg` is checked before `modules`/`externals` in both orders and `isdefined(pkg, name)` is already true for any Base-exported name via Julia's implicit visibility, so the externals/modules ordering is provably unreachable for exactly the names cited (confirmed by an exhaustive measurement over all 421 surface names in the same file's executing#1 finding, which found zero resolution differences); a reader relying on this finding is left with a false belief that the change has real behavioral/cost consequences for consumers when it is inert.

Verified empirically (julia --project): resolve_function(:read, GBGCodingTools, [Config]) returns Base.read not Config.read, and Base has no `report` at all — so the shipped docstring's three named examples and its claim "a package function always wins its own name" are false, meaning a consumer reading and trusting this API contract forms a wrong belief and gets a wrong result.

ARCHITECTURE.md §6.3's closed-vocabulary table goes stale (still lists the old 7-value enum against the new 11-value schema) and the CHANGELOG omits the widening while classifying the release MINOR even though the project's own rule makes any closed-vocabulary change MAJOR — a contradiction between surfaces plus a missing load-bearing statement, not a directly wrong computed result.

The evidence is concrete and verified (fixture measured: 0 rows, 0 extension-homed, so both assertions reduce to 8>0 and 8>=0, true with or without the fix): the newly added test is tautological on the fixture it runs against and cannot detect a regression of the population counter that itself decides DEAD/exit-2, a load-bearing behavior — a real, plausibly-hit gap (any future edit to the counter passes silently) rather than a merely cosmetic or localized wording issue, but it is a test-discrimination defect, not a currently-wrong mathematical/API/cost claim, so it falls short of blocker.

The false claim is confined to a fixture docstring's illustrative narrative (a secondary, test-only surface, not policy/architecture/API docs read by consumers), it produces 0 hits either way so no test result is corrupted, and the finding itself confirms the underlying parser fix is genuinely warranted via two real victims found elsewhere — the planted case simply fails to discriminate old-vs-new, it doesn't cause a wrong belief about the tool's actual behavior or mislead any test outcome.

The test's own comment claims the guard never flags valid JavaScript, but the regex's lookbehind on the preceding character class (not escape state) makes it a false positive on the common `return `...`` / ternary `:` idiom — a real, plausibly-hit defect (a future Workflow script author gets a red Pkg.test() over valid JS) plus an under-covered false-negative direction, not merely a cosmetic or narrow wording gap.

The defect is confined to a comment in a test file (test/schemas.jl) misdescribing history as "pinning a regression" when the validation and the projection it exercises were both introduced fresh in this change set; the test's assertion itself is admitted to be harmless/correct, and the accurate account sits right next to it in Rounds.jl's own comment, so this is inaccurate provenance wording with a nearby correction rather than a false belief about the API, math, or cost that a reader would act on.

The core claim — CFG.SURFACES no longer directly requires docs/make.jl — is real and correctly diagnosed, but the finding's own evidence shows WIRE.MAKEDOCS (NON_EXEMPTABLE, in QUICK) still hardcodes and enforces that exact path in the doctor flow, so the loosening is shadowed for the primary usage path; the residual exposure is the narrower claim (buried in why_it_matters, not carried into the nit conclusion) that Config.read/check_paths can be invoked directly without a doctor run (Step-0 scratch configs, Config.parse), where the two checks would genuinely disagree — a real but localized and only plausibly-hit gap, not a contradiction a typical reader/consumer would encounter.

The evidence shows a real, verified behavior change — SCAN.MATHBF now hardcodes `\mathbf{1}` into every consumer's allowed set regardless of that consumer's `notation.mathbf_allowed` config, so a value the config explicitly forbids now passes a hard (exit-1) scan silently, with no ledger/exemption entry and no CHANGELOG note; this is effectively an unrecorded change to the config's non-configurable set, which this package's own CLAUDE.md/ARCHITECTURE §5.5 treats as a MAJOR-classification event, and two frozen consumers get no signal that the knob stopped meaning what it says — a missing load-bearing statement rather than a case of currently-false prose (the policy/schema text was updated in step with the code, so it doesn't itself mislead a reader).

Verified against source (Passes.jl, Preflight.jl, prose_shape.jl): finding_files' isfile-only resolution genuinely fails on basename-only docstring-unit keys the codebase itself uses for labeling, and on a fix pass that deletes/renames a named file, and covered_paths genuinely excludes root files like CLAUDE.md/README.md/CHANGELOG.md from the 'touched' set pass_scope/unswept rely on — so a closed finding in any of those classes silently keeps its stale verdict while grade()'s tally asserts a re-check that never happened, a real and plausibly-hit gap in the audit tool's own re-verification guarantee (missing load-bearing 'verify when unresolved' invariant) rather than a contrived edge case, but it needs one of several specific location/path shapes to bite rather than being a guaranteed universal wrong result, so blocker overstates it.

The scan's new eltype exemption matches on keyword name alone rather than on the prose-binding the rule requires, so a genuinely undocumented keyword (or any name matching arg_type/hit_type/round_type) now silently passes a hard scan, and the same line simultaneously converts the rule's permission into an obligation for a legitimately-bulleted case — a real, plausibly-hit gap between the rule text and its enforcement, not just cosmetic drift.

The change set edited RULES.toml's statement and ARCHITECTURE to match the scan's actual (unchanged) ratchet-exception behavior but left docs-rubric.md — the exact text `gbg sync` renders into every consumer's `.gbg/policy/`, i.e. the primary reader-facing surface, not a secondary one — saying the stronger "always" wording, so the two canonical statements of RULE.DOC.SHAPE now directly contradict each other where before this window they agreed; that is squarely the "contradiction between surfaces" example the major tier names, even though the code itself did not change and the deeper doc/code drift predates the window.

The lifecycle test is the sole end-to-end driver of pass_open, and the commit that added the sweep gate re-baselined its only success-path assertion to run under sweep_ok=true, leaving the default (no-override) success path — the one a normal session actually takes — checked only by isolated unit tests of unswept/finding_files/pass_scope, not by an integration assertion; a regression in the scope/expected computation would now pass CI silently, which is a real, load-bearing coverage gap on a core verb rather than a cosmetic one.

The reorder and its risk to frozen parity baselines are real (same diff hunk as behaviour-change#4), but this finding's specific undercount path requires a package to both extend a Base generic in one submodule (which binds the same identity as Base's generic, so shadowing is a no-op) and independently define an unrelated own function of the identical name in another submodule — an implausible naming collision with no evidence it exists in any of the four consumers, which the finding itself only credits at "medium confidence"; it adds a speculative sub-case atop an already-reported defect rather than a new load-bearing, plausibly-hit failure.

The underlying change (script-aware check replacing the hardcoded docs/make.jl requirement) is itself a correct fix, and the residual gap — CFG.SURFACES now accepting configs that WIRE.MAKEDOCS would still reject — is a real drift between two validation surfaces, but it only bites for the narrow edge case of a customized docs_build that never invokes docs/make.jl, and only on the non-doctor call paths (Config.parse, Step-0 scratch import); the finding's own "fully shadowed" claim is not even fully consistent with its own why_it_matters, further weakening the case for anything above minor.

The default-on sweep refusal is structurally incompatible with the audit-changes protocol's own no-fix-pass rule, and git history in this exact window (9bd0f00, 07d27fb) confirms it already fired for real — the in-flight audit round hit the refusal and had to be abandoned rather than closed, with the gate left unfixed at HEAD, so the instrument's default path is unusable and the bank hint omits the undocumented --sweep-ok workaround.

The evidence shows a concrete, demonstrated arithmetic defect (denominator over all findings vs numerator over the scoped subset) that silently writes provably wrong numbers (e.g. adjudicated_share=0.0, demoted_by_rule=0 despite real adjudications/demotions existing) into a persisted artifact that gbg fleet --diff reads to compare rounds across versions — a reader/tool consuming this artifact gets a wrong quantified result with no error or flag raised, which is exactly the wrong-result-about-a-computed-quantity case the blocker tier describes, not a stale or localized wording issue.

Verified against the tree: mathbf.jl now hardcodes push!(allowed, "\\mathbf{1}") regardless of cfg, and the rule text, schema description, and config guide were all updated in lockstep to describe the new behavior accurately — so no surface currently misleads a reader, ruling out blocker. But this silently removes a value from a config range CLAUDE.md itself calls a closed per-package variation point ("changing either is MAJOR"), with no CHANGELOG entry anywhere (grep for "mathbf" in CHANGELOG.md finds only an unrelated PF-hard-scan count) and no exemption-ledger/doctor signal — a real, verifiable process gap that a consumer who set mathbf_allowed to exclude \mathbf{1} will plausibly hit (their enforcement quietly stops), which is more than localized wording drift.

A shared-harness resolution-order change silently alters resolve_function's output for any Base-colliding name, propagating into method_parity/allocation/traffic/oracle counts against frozen consumer baselines, with no test, no baseline update, and no migration note in this change set — a real, plausibly-hit defect (frozen oracle failing or a previously-masked 0 count going non-zero) rather than an immediate wrong claim in this package's own docs/tests.

The scan fix correctly matches an already-written, unchanged rule (docs-rubric.md's both-halves text is unchanged since base), so nothing is now factually wrong or misleading — but tightening a hard, build-gating, all-surfaces scan with no CHANGELOG entry or consumer sweep is a missing load-bearing statement that a consumer will plausibly hit as a surprise build failure on the next `gbg bump`, which is a real, plausible defect rather than a cosmetic or localized one.

The reordering is applied consistently across rule, sentinel, hats and ARCHITECTURE (no internal contradiction, so not blocker-level "wrong"), but it is a real, concrete, plausibly-triggered defect: an undocumented fleet-rubric change bundled into an unrelated commit will cause doc-policy/structure-consistency to report false findings against all four frozen corpora in the next /check-docs round, with no migration note or deviation-ledger entry, and the moved LEG.SENTINELS sentinel means a consumer still carrying the old restated text is no longer caught either — a missing load-bearing governance step with a concrete downstream failure mode, not a cosmetic or speculative one.

The claimed catastrophic path (a schema-valid docs_build naming no .jl script, tripping the new check_paths rejection) can't actually reach that branch: schema/config.schema.json's unchanged pattern on package.docs_build requires the literal substring "docs/make.jl", so any config that clears schema validation already yields a non-empty scripts list before check_paths ever runs (Config.parse's order is schema validate -> materialize! -> check_paths, and Doctor.jl's only other call site uses an already-validated cfg). The test exercising the empty-scripts branch calls check_paths directly on a hand-built Dict that bypasses schema — not a path any real consumer config can take. The ARCHITECTURE.md wording relaxation is accurate; the new rejection, though genuinely untested, is dead in practice, so this is a real but practically unreachable gap rather than a defect an operator will plausibly hit.

The splat-counting change silently widens what RULE.DOC.ARGS_FORM (text unchanged) counts as a keyword parameter, so every fleet docstring of the shape f(x; kwargs...) written in prose now trips a new false-positive triage hit with no rule support, no fixture case, and no test — a real, reproducible defect an operator will plausibly hit across corpora, not a one-off wording slip.

The evidence shows a concrete contradiction between surfaces: pass_open's unconditional sweep guard (quoted code) will always fire for audit-changes rounds given the protocol's own documented step-4 design ("never edits the tree"), and unlike check-docs/check-consistency, audit-changes/PROTOCOL.md was not updated to name the resulting --sweep-ok requirement — a missing load-bearing statement plus a plausibly-hit operational defect, matching the major tier rather than a text-level wrong-belief blocker.

The evidence shows finding_files scans the whole tree while touched is restricted to covered_paths (directories only, per Config.jl:203), so any finding quoting a root-level non-directory file (CHANGELOG.md, README.md, fleet.toml, etc.) can never be swept — a genuinely complete fix is permanently reported as missed, and the only escape is --sweep-ok, which disables the check for every other finding in the pass too; since the release checklist itself requires a CHANGELOG.md entry per round, this is a plausibly-common case, not an edge case, and it defeats the guard's stated purpose rather than merely misfiring cosmetically.

Verified in Passes.jl: unswept's skip list only excludes seeded/scans-lane ids (line 123), grade's closure channels are honored/adjudicated/seeded/rescan only (deferral alone never sets closed_by, confirmed at lines ~350-420), and close() requires open_ids empty (line 579) — so any deferred finding must also be adjudicated to close the round, yet an adjudicated id's named files are deliberately untouched and pass_open's unswept check (not skipping it) will refuse the pass (exit 2) whenever that id is still counted open going into a pass, forcing --sweep-ok to blanket-disable the check for every other finding in that pass too; this is a real, newly-introduced regression that plausibly fires on any normal round using the design's own adjudication/deferral channels, but it's a workflow refusal with a documented escape hatch rather than a silent wrong result, so major rather than blocker.

The coverage gap is real and accurately quoted (verified against git show at both commits: pass_open's == 0 assertion did become == 2 plus a sweep_ok=true override, and no test calls pass_open with a genuine sweep and no override), but it is narrow: the same test file's adjacent 'refuses an unswept fix' testset already exercises unswept() directly in both directions (fires on a half-fix, silent when fully swept), and pass_open's wiring around it is a single `if !sweep_ok` gate, so the risk of an undetected regression is low — a nearby-corrected coverage thinness, not a defect a maintainer would plausibly hit or be misled by.

Verified in source: the schema's occursin-based pattern guarantees every schema-valid docs_build already contains "docs/make.jl", making the new isempty(scripts) branch provably dead, while the new per-token regex naively splits on whitespace/quotes and will false-positive on any other .jl-suffixed token (a --project= path ending in a Julia-convention ".jl" directory, or a quoted path containing a space, which this project's own conventions require) — and this same check_paths is called by Doctor's CFG.SURFACES, which is in QUICK and gates TestHarness.gate() and the makedocs wrapper, so a false hit breaks the build for a previously-passing consumer; the accompanying test also only reaches the new branches via a hand-built cfg dict the schema would itself reject, confirming a real contradiction between the schema and check_paths surfaces rather than a reachable real-world path.

The regex `\Q\Esite` has no terminator, so it prefix-matches any URL under the sibling's site (confirmed by direct code inspection); paired with the new later-mention-must-be-bare-code-span rule at hard tier, this will plausibly reject legitimate deep links (e.g. to a specific API page) written after a package's first mention, breaking `gbg scan docs`/`makedocs`/round prepare for prose that is not actually violating the rule's intent — a real, code-verified defect a docs author will plausibly hit, but it misapplies a scan rather than asserting a false mathematical/API/cost claim, so it falls short of blocker.

The change is a real widening of a triage-tier (non-blocking) lint's argument-counting logic that can misclassify a kwargs... pass-through wrapper as needing bulleted docs, but it produces only a warning-level false positive on doc formatting, not a wrong belief about the API, math, or cost, and the finding's own evidence confirms the tier is non-failing in both base and head.

The reorder is a real, verifiable behavior change that flips a previously population>0/passing configuration (all-extension-homed exports) into a DEAD/exit-2 refusal, and the only oracle added asserts just the positive-count case, leaving the newly reachable failure path untested and its message lacking any ledger/remedy route — a genuine defect a consumer could plausibly hit, even though the underlying logic change is defensible on its own terms.

Verified in source: cmd_sync (gbg sync) calls sync()->status()->read_sidecar() with no local catch, so the new schema's SyncError falls through to main()'s generic handler as exit 3 (crash, backtrace printed) instead of exit 2, while Doctor.jl's sync_status wraps the identical call in try/catch to degrade gracefully -- a real, self-admitted (per the quoted CHANGELOG) regression a consumer upgrading with a pre-existing managed.json will plausibly hit, but it surfaces as a loud crash with a remediation message rather than a silent wrong result/belief, so major rather than blocker.

Verified via git diff that resolve_function's search order genuinely flipped (externals-before-modules -> modules-before-externals) in a shared, frozen TestHarness primitive that method_parity/oracle_registry use to resolve names for frozen baselines, with zero test coverage anywhere in the repo (no baseline files exist, no test/ hits) and no CHANGELOG mention despite the Unreleased section logging other changes from this same diff -- a missing load-bearing statement about a consequential instrument behavior change. It stops short of blocker because the new docstring is itself accurate and the reorder is a genuine, well-justified bug fix, and no consumer is currently broken (consumers stay frozen until migration and no baseline artifacts exist yet in this repo), so no reader is misled today -- the risk is a plausible future one when consumers migrate and pin baselines, matching major rather than blocker.

pass_open's default now flips a previously-succeeding call to a hard refusal (exit 0 -> 2) for any round that didn't touch every finding's location -- a real breaking change to the CLI's public contract -- and CHANGELOG.md, which the project's own header asserts is the complete per-release record, says nothing about it, so a reader checking the changelog for breaking changes would miss this one; it stays short of blocker because the behavior is correctly documented elsewhere (docstring, ARCHITECTURE.md), so no surface actively states something false.

The evidence shows an intentional, well-tested fix closing a genuine prior gap (core schema was never checked at bank time); the complaint is only that the refusal surfaces late in a costly workflow — a UX/cost-sequencing tradeoff, not a wrong or misleading claim about behavior, API, or math, and not a contradiction between surfaces.

The finding's own evidence shows the stricter scan rule, its RULES.toml/catalog wording, and its fixture are all mutually consistent and intentional — no contradiction between surfaces, no stale claim, no missing statement — so this is a deliberate, correctly-implemented lint tightening (the kind any consumer must adapt to) rather than something misleading; the real compatibility-impact concern is an adjacent versioning/disclosure question already covered by a separate finding (invariants#1), not a defect in this scan or its documentation.

Verified in src/CLI/Passes.jl: demoted/adjudicated are reset per pass and incremented only over the scoped findings subset, while the denominator (all_findings) and closed were correctly widened to the full cumulative per_id map, so demoted_by_rule/adjudicated_share silently undercount from pass 2 of any scoped round onward — a real, plausibly-hit, verified numeric bug affecting a reported statistic (consumed by gbg fleet --diff), but it does not corrupt the round's actual gate decision (open_ids/closed/exit code), making it a stale/wrong quantified claim rather than a wrong core result.

The regex exemption is provably broader than the rubric's written "element-type keyword" exemption (it matches any _type-suffixed identifier like return_type/cache_type/sort_type), causing SCAN.ARGS_FORM to silently under-report docstrings that should require bulleted form -- a real, plausibly-hit defect in the instrument's own enforcement of the rule it cites, though it degrades doc-formatting triage rather than misstating math, an API contract, or a cost.

A genuine contradiction between two surfaces of the same package — §5.5's unqualified "changing any vocabulary/schema is MAJOR" versus the CHANGELOG's own "MINOR so far" label on a diff that (by the diff and Sync.jl's own updated docstring) breaks previously-valid sidecars from an older release — but it stops short of blocker because the CHANGELOG entry is explicitly provisional (still under Unreleased, flagged "so far") rather than a finalized, shipped claim that has already misled a reader into a wrong belief or action.

The diff and docstring update are accurate (verified against the commit), so no reader is misled by the text itself — but the finding correctly shows a fleet-wide, silently behavior-changing edit to the frozen-baseline method_parity contract landed in Unreleased with zero CHANGELOG mention (unlike the sibling schema-tightening entry right above it), a missing load-bearing disclosure that a downstream consumer could plausibly hit as an unexplained Pkg.test() break on bump — major rather than blocker since nothing in the text is wrong or misleading per se.

The commit message overclaims three code-level fixes when only two landed (the resolve_function docstring edit merely re-describes the same still-buggy loop order), producing a false 'honored' disposition in the pass audit trail that let the actual Base-shadowing bug persist uncaught for several more commits; but the docstring text itself still accurately describes the code's actual (buggy) order at that commit, so a reader isn't misled about the API's current search order from the docs alone — only about the fix's provenance/status, matching a contradiction-between-surfaces / stale-claim defect rather than a directly wrong belief about the mathematics or API behavior itself.

It is a real miscount in a commit-message log claim (11 vs 8 files) but a secondary, historical surface with no live doc or API impact — all eight edits it describes are real and complete, nothing is missing or broken, so it's unlikely to mislead a reader about the codebase's actual state.

The same paragraph of policy/testing-protocol.md now both defines "session" as "a working agreement no artefact records" and calls it (with "panel") "an answer" satisfying RULE.TEST.RULE_WITH_CHECK, while two sentences later the surviving original text says exactly that condition ("someone remembering this rule") "is not enforcement" — a direct self-contradiction that reclassifies 25 previously-declared known weaknesses (a debt/cost accounting) as satisfied across every consumer that pins this policy, with the new test verifying only that a label string is present, not that any check exists.

The docstring order rewrite leaves two normative rendered-policy surfaces (RULE.DOC.HOME_ORDER's new order and RULE.CIT.FULL_INLINE's unchanged "at its end" citation placement) both claiming the terminal slot for a docstring with a load-bearing caveat and a citation — a genuine contradiction between surfaces that any of the four consumer packages' docstring authors, writing exactly the formula+caveat+citation shape this rubric targets, can plausibly hit, and the rule's check is recorded as "weakness" so nothing catches the collision.

A new binding fleet rule (no mid-round correction) was folded into an existing rule's paragraph without its own id/statement/sentinel, so RULE.INST.AUDIT_AFTER_CODE's RULES.toml register still states only the old requirement — a real contradiction between the authoritative register and the actual policy text — and the inherited check (test:test/rounds.jl) will be read as covering the new rule though nothing in it exercises the no-correction behavior, leaving this new fleet-wide constraint invisible to LEG.SENTINELS, the ledger, and any doctor/scan going forward.

With the scan's code byte-identical, the fleet-facing policy/RULES.toml statement of RULE.DOC.SHAPE had its "always" quantifier and its caveat naming re-baselining as an escape silently dropped for a quieter ratchet-only exemption on baselined units, with no ledger/weakness entry recording the loosened promise, and the same change set immediately exercises that exemption by re-baselining docs/prose_shape.csv past the old nominal cap — a real, load-bearing drift (stale quantified claim plus missing debt record) in a rule rendered into four consumers' policy, but a process/contract-integrity gap rather than text that hands a reader a wrong mathematical, API, or cost result.

RULES.toml's RULE.TEX.MATHBF statement (and its LEG.SENTINELS sentinel) is the load-bearing register text cited by ledger entries and instruments, and it still asserts mathbf_allowed is the whole answer while the scan code now unconditionally admits \mathbf{1} regardless of that config — a real, plausibly-hit contradiction between the code surface and the authoritative rule-id surface, not just a stale wording nit.

A closed vocabulary (state enum) was widened in the schema but ARCHITECTURE §6.3's table — the authoritative vocabulary listing that CLAUDE.md itself says is MAJOR to change, and whose own text instructs consumers to audit their code against it before adopting — was left showing the old 6-value set against the new 10-value schema; that's a direct contradiction between two authoritative surfaces (schema vs. design doc) with a load-bearing consequence (a consumer following §6.3's audit instruction checks against a stale list and can miss real closed-switch bugs on the new PASS/FAIL/BROKEN/BLOCKED values), matching the rubric's own major example of "a contradiction between surfaces, a stale quantified claim" rather than a wrong mathematical/API result stated outright (blocker) or a localized/secondary-surface gap (minor).

The behavioral change (CFG.SURFACES no longer requires docs_build to specifically be docs/make.jl) is disclosed consistently at both cited ARCHITECTURE.md locations and matches the code, so there is no contradiction or stale claim to mislead a reader; the residual complaint is a speculative, unconfirmed gap (whether WIRE.MAKEDOCS/D9 still enforce docs/make.jl some other way) rather than a demonstrated contradiction or missing load-bearing statement.

The deleted comment was the only record in the tree of a failure mode that had already occurred (reflection scans silently skipping and reporting clean if GBGFixture drops out of test/Project.toml); its loss is a missing load-bearing statement that a future editor tidying that file could plausibly hit, even though nothing is currently false or contradictory.

Confirmed by diff/git-show evidence: RULES.toml's statement and ARCHITECTURE §12.B were updated to the relaxed ratchet-scoping rule, but the source paragraph in policy/docs-rubric.md (which RULES.toml is supposed to be regenerated from, per the tool's own D12 invariant) and the twin rule-id row in ARCHITECTURE §12.A were left byte-identical to base — a genuine contradiction between surfaces describing the same rule, exactly the "major" category (contradiction between surfaces / stale statement), even though the underlying scan code itself is unaffected.

The diff changed the actual mathbf{1} exemption behavior and updated the scan, latex-idiom.md, and ARCHITECTURE §12.B, but left RULES.toml's one-line statement, ARCHITECTURE §12.A's mirror, and the latex-typesetter hat's persona stating the old conditional rule — a well-evidenced contradiction between authoritative surfaces (including a persona an LLM hat instrument actually consults), matching the 'contradiction between surfaces' major criterion rather than blocker since the scan itself, the primary enforcement path, is correct.

Verified live: testing-protocol.md's new self-referential text and RULES.toml's check=["panel"] for RULE.API.POSITIONAL explicitly retire the "known weakness" label for exactly this case, yet CLAUDE.md:5 (touched by this same diff, sha changed) still asserts "has no check anywhere and is a KNOWN WEAKNESS" — a genuine contradiction between surfaces in the package's own governing texts, but it misstates a policy/enforcement classification rather than a mathematical result, API behavior, or cost, so it falls short of blocker.

IMPLEMENTATION.md's CLI-signature table for `pass open` now contradicts the actual usage string, ARCHITECTURE.md, and two instrument protocols by omitting `--sweep-ok` and the refusal behavior it gates — a real cross-surface contradiction and missing load-bearing statement for anyone consulting the build-plan table as the CLI reference, but the live CLI usage string itself is correct, so no one is misled into a wrong action, just a wrong belief about the documented spec.

The dead RULE./SCAN. references and out-of-place scanner-rationale are real rubric violations, but they sit inside a toy fixture function used only to exercise the test suite, not in any shipped or reader-facing consumer documentation, so no actual API/doc reader plausibly hits this confusion — the risk is confined to a single isolated internal test artifact.
